title: Chapter 163 – The Lamplighter's Heir
html:
[The Hall of the Sixth Door – Lin Jian]

By the sixth day he can walk to the end of the corridor and back without Bell's arm, and she pretends not to watch.

It is a small victory. He takes it. The staff taps on the boards, and the long pale gown trails after, and every thirty paces he stops to lean on a wall and let the dizziness pass. There are fewer lamps than there were. He counts them as he goes, a habit he has caught from Yue: two hundred and sixty-three, said Nurse, a week ago. Now, by his own tally, there are two hundred and forty. Where the missing ones hung, the dark stands in the air like a held breath.

You're doing it again, says the boy.

What?

Counting. Like it's going to help.

It helps me.

It makes you sad. A pause. But I do it too. I counted the stairs.

How many?

Two hundred and twelve. The boy's voice is thin and amused. I was glad to be right.

Jian smiles. He turns at the end of the corridor, where the ring of light curves out of sight, and begins the walk back. Ahead of him, at the open door of the Annex, Ao is sitting on the sill with the rabbit in his lap, and he waves, a quick fierce wave, as if Jian has come home from a long war.

It is the nicest thing that has happened to him in a month.

* * *

Bell catches him alone that evening, at the washstand, with a cup of the black wax tea in her hands.

"Drink," she says.

He drinks. It is as foul as the pills. She watches him finish it with her arms folded, and when the cup is empty, she takes it, and sets it down on the shelf, and says, "I want the numbers."

"Which numbers?"

"The ones you have not told me." Her voice is level. "Do not insult me, Jian. I have been in the room with you for nine days. You cough in the night. You hide the handkerchief. You do not eat what I give you. You asked me on the first day whether I could keep you alive, and I said yes, and you did not ask again. That is not a man who thinks he has years."

He considers lying. It would be easy. She would see it, and she would be kind about it, and he would owe her an apology on top of the lie.

"The panel gave me a figure," he says. "On the day I arrived. Nine tenths of a year. It has not been recalculated since. But I think it is lower now."

"How much lower?"

"I do not know."

"Guess."

"Six months." The words are very quiet. "Perhaps five."

Bell nods slowly. She looks at her hands. Then she crosses the cell and sits down on the edge of the cot and puts her arm round his shoulders, stiffly, the way she would hold a patient she has decided to love.

"Then we will make them good months," she says.

"Bell—"

"Hush. I am a healer. I know what to do with a number." She squeezes once. "You will stop walking so far. You will sleep when I tell you. And you will let the children help."

He leans, a little, into her shoulder. It is bony and warm and smells of herbs.

"Yes," he says.

* * *

Ethan sends for them at the turn of the afternoon.

He does not use the grille this time. He uses Nurse, who comes to the door of Jian's cell with her hands tucked in her apron and says, in her soft precise voice, that Mr. Cole has been awake since the third watch and has something to say, and would prefer to say it with the girl listening.

They go down together, all of them, because nobody wants to be left. Bell takes his left arm and Yue his right. Ao and Tao come behind, hand in hand, with Mo Yan walking a little apart, her stub of charcoal clenched in one fist. At the head of the stair the mist rolls out to meet them. The bridge hums.

The shaft is darker than he has ever seen it.

The milk-white light that once rose in ropes has thinned to a pale haze, hardly brighter than moonlight. The walls of the glass chamber are clouded. Ethan Cole sits in the middle of it, still cross-legged, still with his hands cupped upward, but he has aged. The wire under his skin has dimmed. His cheeks are hollowed. His eyes, when they open, are pale and wet and very tired.

Come in, he says. Come in, all of you. Mei wants to see the little ones.

Cupped in his hands, almost lost in the gloom, floats a single bright seed of light. No larger than a pea. No bigger than the head of a pin.

Hello, says a voice, so soft that Jian has to lean forward to hear it. Hello, Ao. Hello, Tao. Hello, Mo Yan. I wanted to look at you.

Ao steps forward without a word. He stands at the edge of the platform with the rabbit hugged to his chest and looks into the glass. Then, quite formally, he bows.

Thank you, says Mei. That's very polite.

* * *

I have to tell you something, Ethan says, when the children have been led back up the stair by Nurse and only the four of them remain. I have done the sum. I am afraid it comes out badly.

"Tell it plainly," says Jian.

Mei's coherence is at fifty-one percent. She will give you one more wake. After that, she needs a rest of eight to ten days, or she will not recover. He swallows. There are four sleepers left. Each costs between eleven and twenty percent. If you wake all four at once, we lose her.

"Eight days of rest," Bell says. "We have thirty-one before the first of the beasts arrive."

Yes.

"We have a longer road home than that."

Yes. Ethan's mouth works. I know. I have been doing nothing but arithmetic since the second wake, and I cannot make the figures meet. If you wake them all, you lose the girl. If you leave them sleeping, they cannot walk out of the Hall with you. And if you take any of them out at all, the Hall will lose them from the cradles, and they will lose the Hall.

"What does that mean?" Yue asks. Bell writes it on the slate.

The beds are tuned to them. Ethan lifts his eyes. Each child's pattern is bound to the room. If you carry one out into the world, the pattern frays. They will live, for a time. A year, perhaps. And then they will fade.

The silence is complete.

"Then it was never possible," says Jian slowly. "To wake them and take them home."

It was possible for you. You were never tied to the beds. You were born. A bitter smile. I made the others to sleep. Only you were made to walk.

* * *

Jian goes to the lip of the bridge and stands looking down into the dim shaft for a long time.

He thinks of Ao's hand, and the weight of the rabbit's paw in his own. He thinks of Tao's anger, and Mo Yan's silver bell. He thinks of a ledger with a cracked blue cover, and of thirty-one beds that went quiet in a night. He thinks, without wanting to, of the long white road he walked here, and of the people on it, and of the sixty days.

Brother, says the boy, very quietly. You can't keep them all.

I know.

You can't save the Hall and the valley both.

I know.

Then what do you want?

He opens his mouth to answer. And finds that he does not know.

It is a strange feeling. For a hundred and nineteen years he has always known. When he was a boy in the Lin clan, he knew he wanted to live. When he was a young man, he knew he wanted to protect. When he came to the Sixth Door, he knew he wanted to find the sleepers. He has never before stood at the edge of a bridge and not felt a pull in one direction or another.

I want, he says at last, slowly, to be asked.

Asked?

I would like someone to tell me what they want. And then I would like to do it.

A sound behind him. Ethan Cole is laughing, a thin wet breathy laugh, with his face in his shoulder. That, he says, is the first sensible thing anyone has said in this room in six hundred years.

* * *

They put it to the children at the table.

It is Nurse who proposes it, and Bell who quietly seconds. The Annex is warm with the smell of rice, and the seven cots are lined up in their half circle. At the round table in the middle, which Nurse has cleared, sit the three who are awake. Ao and Tao on one bench, side by side, their feet not reaching the floor. Mo Yan on a stool with her charcoal. Yue sits at the end, her hand resting lightly on the child's wrist, her face intent. Jian sits opposite them, and the empty chairs beside him are for the four who still sleep.

He lays it out in simple words.

He tells them that the Hall is failing. He tells them that the beds are tied to them, and that they cannot go home. He tells them that there are four more who need waking, and that Mei can only give one more now, and that the rest must wait. He tells them that in thirty-one days something terrible will come up from below, and that he does not know whether the Hall can stand.

When he is finished, nobody speaks.

Tao is the first. He puts down his spoon and says, in a clear furious voice, "We're not leaving."

"Tao—"

"We're not. We were here first." He scowls. "Papa's here. Mei's here. Nurse is here. Where would we go?"

"To a valley," Jian says, "where there is a tree."

"I don't want a tree."

Ao nudges him. Ao's voice is small and level. I want to see it, he says. But I want to come back.

Tao opens his mouth, closes it, and stares at the table.

Mo Yan, who has not stirred, reaches out and takes Yue's slate. She writes, in a stiff cramped hand that Jian has not seen before, a single line.

Wake the one who holds the lamp.

Jian reads it twice.

"Zhen Li?"

She nods. She underlines the sentence. Then she writes, underneath, so fast that the chalk squeaks, He can fix the lights.

* * *

Ethan asks for him, alone, in the thin hours of the night after the council.

He goes down the stair by himself, one tread at a time, with the lamp in his left hand and the staff in his right. The bridge hums. The shaft is nearly black. When he reaches the platform, he sees the pea-sized spark in the old man's palms, and the old man himself, haggard and gray, his chin sunk on his breast.

I am sorry to wake you, says Ethan. I hoped you would be awake.

"I was."

Of course you were. A weak smile. Sit. Please. I have something to say, and it is not for the children.

Jian sits on the cushions. He folds his hands on the crook of the staff.

It is about Mei's choice. Ethan's voice is low. The one she promised to make after Ao woke. She has told me what it is. I think you should know before she tells you, so that you can decide whether to let her.

"Tell me."

She will say no to the tree. The old man closes his eyes. She will say that she would rather stay as she is, in the Gate, with her father, and the light, and the sleepers, than live in a root in a valley she has never seen. She will say that a cradle is still a cage. He draws a long shuddering breath. And I think she is right. But if she says it, I will not be able to hold the Gate. I am not strong enough to stand between her and the end.

"Then she will die."

In a few weeks, yes. As the Hall dies. The gray eyes open. I wanted to ask you to talk her out of it.

"No."

Jian—

"No." He says it gently. "I will not ask her to choose against herself. I did that once, when I was a boy, to the voice in my head. I told him he could stay, and I did not mean it, and I have never forgiven myself." His throat is tight. "She has been asked to hold a world for six hundred years, Ethan. If she wants to put it down, I will help her put it down."

The old man stares at him. Then, slowly, to Jian's astonishment, he begins to laugh again, silently, helplessly, with tears running down his tired face.

Oh, you're so like her, he says. You're so very like her.

* * *

Ethan is dubious. Nurse is more so.

They argue it in the corridor, in low voices, with the children out of hearing. The Lamplighters were a house of hereditary keepers, says Ethan, through the grille. Before the Hall, in the Gate's early years. They tended the beacon on the surface, and later the beacons in the dome. Zhen Li's father kept them for forty years. It was a small trade. A family occupation. I did not choose him for his lamps.

"Why did you choose him?" asks Bell.

Because the copy took. A pause. He was eleven, and he was frightened of the dark, and I thought that a boy who feared the dark would be gentle. I was wrong about the fear, I think. I did not understand what the lamp meant to him.

"What does it mean?"

I have no idea.

Nurse says, thoughtfully, "He sleeps with it, you know. The lamp. It is not in the bed. It is in his arms. When he came to us, he would not put it down for the lamps in the Annex. He said they were not his."

"Not his."

"I mended its wick myself, in the fourth year. A strange wick. It did not burn oil." She hesitates. "It burned something else. And it did not go out."

Jian looks at her.

"Mo Yan thinks he can fix the lights," he says.

"Mo Yan hears things that nobody else hears," says Nurse. "I have never known her to be wrong."

* * *

Nurse sits with Zhen Li the night before.

Jian is not meant to be there. He is passing the Annex door on his way to bed when he hears her voice, low and calm, and he stops in the shadow of the corridor with his hand on the wall. Through the gap in the door he can see the two of them: the small round woman in her apron, and the pale sleeping boy on the fourth cot, whom she has taken by the hand.

"I do not know if you can hear me," she is saying. "But I have always spoken to you all, in the evenings, and it would be strange to stop. I want to tell you what has happened. You have missed a good deal."

She tells him about the Gate. About the old man in the well. About the girl who gave her voice to the lamps. About the old copy, Lin Jian, who walked a hundred and nineteen years to find them. She tells it slowly, plainly, in the voice she must have used a thousand times, and Jian realizes with a pang that every night for six hundred years she has told seven sleepers the day's news, and has never once had an answer.

"I want you to know that I am sorry," she says. "I let the lamps go. I did not know how to keep them. Your father taught me the rule, and I forgot it, in the long years. I thought it was a small thing."

She smooths the blanket.

"If you wake, I will not ask you to forgive me. I will only ask you to teach me again."

Jian goes quietly down the corridor to bed. He does not trust himself to speak.

* * *

The wake is simple, as these things go.

Mei gives the last of what she can spare. It costs her eleven percent, the lowest of the four, and the seed in her father's palms dims from a pea to a pin. No one speaks of it. Yue stays in the Annex with her hand on Mo Yan's wrist, and Bell stands at the foot of the bed with the reed and flask ready, and Jian lies on the eighth cot with the old rabbit's paw in his hand, as before.

Zhen Li wakes quietly.

There is no gasp, no shout, no sob. A boy of eleven opens his eyes, and the first thing he does is look for the brass lamp. It is in the crook of his arm. He finds it with his fingers before he finds the ceiling. A small round thing, tarnished at the seams, with a spout like a duck's bill. He holds it to his chest and exhales.

"It's out," he says.

His voice is flat, and a little hoarse, and not afraid. He sits up and looks round the Annex with calm gray eyes. He sees the cots, the children, the stove, the dark lamps on the wall. He frowns.

"They're all out," he says. "Why are they out?"

Nurse is by his side before Jian can answer. She takes his shoulders and says, very gently, that the Hall is weak, and the old fire has gone low, and the lamps have been fading for many months.

"How many months?"

"Years," Nurse says. "Hundreds of them."

The boy's face does not change. But something in his hands does. They tighten on the brass lamp, and for a moment the lamp's dull sides give back a thin gleam, orange as a candle, as if some inner thing had stirred.

"That's not right," he says. "They don't go out. They can't. My father said. The first rule of the Lamplighters: you never let the last lamp go." He looks up at Jian, and for the first time his young face is hard. "Who was keeping them?"

"No one," Jian says. "For a very long time. Until you."

"Then it's my fault."

"It is not."

"It is." Zhen Li slides off the cot. He is small for eleven, thin as a rail, with a shock of black hair that stands up at the back. He stands in the middle of the Annex floor in his bare feet and holds the lamp in front of him in both hands. "I fell asleep. I wasn't supposed to."

He closes his eyes.

* * *

He does it at the center of the corridor, in the dark.

Jian watches from the end with the staff in his hand and Bell at his elbow. The boy walks up the ring of light until he reaches the first of the dead lamps, a brass fixture high on the wall, dull and cold as stone. He stops. He lifts the brass lamp in his small hands, and holds it up toward the fixture, and says something Jian cannot catch.

The lamp in his hands brightens.

It is not a bright light. It is a pale orange glow, the color of a coal. But it spreads. It spills over the boy's fingers and runs up his forearms, and in the dark above him the dead fixture shivers. A spark leaps from the brass lamp's spout, a tiny bead of fire, and floats up, and touches the wick of the one on the wall.

It catches.

A flame. A small, steady, golden flame, in a lamp that has been dark for a hundred years. The light flows out along the corridor, warm and amber, and the dark pulls back as if scalded.

Zhen Li lowers the brass lamp. His face is wet. He does not wipe it.

"One," he says.

And he walks to the next.

Jian reads the panel twice. His chest is very cold.

"Stop him," he says.

Bell looks at him. "What?"

"Stop him. Each lamp costs him a memory. His own. He is lighting them with his life."

She is already moving. But Zhen Li has reached the second lamp, and the third, and a light is growing down the corridor like dawn. He walks steadily, one lamp after another, and the tarnished brass in his hands burns ever hotter. Jian goes after him, as fast as the staff and his failing legs will allow, and reaches him at the sixth.

"Zhen Li."

The boy does not turn.

"Zhen Li, stop. Please. It is costing you."

"I know." His voice is very steady. "It always costs. That's what the lamp is for."

"What did you give it?"

"My mother's name." The boy lifts the brass lamp to the seventh fixture. "And the way my father whistled. And the color of the door at home." He says it as if reading a list. "I don't mind. They're only mine. And the lamps are everyone's."

He lights the seventh.

* * *

Jian takes the boy's wrist, finally, and holds it, and Zhen Li lets him.

They stand together in the long amber corridor, with eight lamps burning and two hundred and ten still dark. The boy is shivering. His eyes are enormous in the new light, and he is watching Jian's face with a solemn child's patience. Behind them the others have gathered, Bell and Yue and the three small ones, and nobody speaks.

"It is a good thing you do," says Jian, at last. "I will not stop you. It is not mine to stop. But I will not let you do it alone, and I will not let you do it for nothing." He draws a breath. "Tell me what the lamps are for."

"For the beasts," says Zhen Li.

"The beasts."

"They don't come for the noise. They don't come for the pain." The brass lamp glows in his hands, and he looks down at it. "They come for the dark. Every lamp that goes out opens a corridor. My father said that was the real reason for the Lamplighters. Not to see. To keep the way shut."

Jian goes still.

"Say that again."

"The beasts come when the lamps go out." The boy lifts his gaze. "Didn't anyone tell you? There are two hundred and ten dark. If they all go, there will be no wall left in the whole Hall."

Oh, says the boy in Jian's chest. Oh, brother. It was never about the Gate.

No.

It was about the light.

Down the long corridor, in the dark patch beyond the seventh lamp, something moves. A shape in the shadow, patient and vast and slow. It is not a beast, not yet. It is only the place where a beast will be.

Zhen Li lifts the brass lamp in both hands and walks toward it.
